newsitem.title: UK: London gold retreats ahead of Swiss sales plan.
newsitem.headline: London gold retreats ahead of Swiss sales plan.

text.p: Gold prices fell on Wednesday as a proposal from the ultra-conservative Swiss National Bank to sell gold from its reserves over 10 years came on top of dwindling confidence about the metal's recent rally, dealers said.
Gold fixed at $355.75 per ounce, down from $359.40 on Tuesday and $362.15 on March 3, its highest fixing since January 3 this year.
As recently as February 12 gold fixed at a 3-3/4 year low of $336.90.
Swiss President Arnold Koller proposed that the fund should be capitalised at about seven billion Swiss francs, equivalent to about US$4.7 billion.
Some analysts translated that as meaning Switzerland would sell about 40 tonnes of gold a year to raise investment capital for the fund.

The Swiss proposal involved using official gold reserves to create a humanitarian fund for victims of the Holocaust and other tragedies and would entail selling the gold over a 10-year period, according to Swiss National bank chairman Hans Meyer.
He told a Zurich news conference sales would not disrupt the gold market and had no implications for the stability of the Swiss franc.

Ted Arnold, metals market analyst at Merrill Lynch, described the tonnage as "a drop in the ocean" for a market that has a daily turnover of around 900 tonnes, according to data from the London Bullion Market Association.
Even so, dealers reacted bearishly to the news, which comes on top of a faltering in the sentiment that took prices from their recent low,
"The amount is not huge by any means but it is indicative of central bank sentiment towards the market," one senior bullion dealer said.

Gold prices began to weaken late last year on concerns that European central banks would mobilise their gold reserves as part of their strategy to meet European Monetary Union convergence criteria ahead of the European Union establishing a single currency.
Rumours of national bank sales swept the market, wrecking sentiment and taking prices to February's low.
The previous month, the Dutch central bank announced it had sold 300 tonnes from its reserves. When no further similar announcements followed, the price and sentiment began to revive.

The investment funds which had built huge short positions -- sold gold that they did not own on the basis of buying for delivery at cheaper prices in the future -- had to start covering these positions and the price began to rise.
"The market turned bullish on the fact that there were no more central bank sales. Now the Swiss news has turned it again," said Arnold.
However, some dealers conceded that at recent levels above $360.00, the gold price was beginning to look "toppy".
"Gold had a short-covering rally and now that that is over we could see the lows again," one dealer said.
The legislation necessary to allow the Swiss move would take about two years, according to Meyer.
Swiss gold reserves are valued currently at Swiss francs 4,595 per kg and would need to be revalued by almost four times to meet current market value.
"On the basis of a more realistic -- albeit still cautious -- valuation, several billion francs could be transferred in gold to the foundation," Meyer said.

Late last year gold market confidence slumped on another proposal from Switzerland that it begin the process of referendum, legislation and constitutional change to end its need to have 40 percent of its note issue backed with gold.
Prices were weaker in the other precious metals. Silver followed gold to be three cents easier from Tuesday at $5.21/$5.23.
Platinum was $4.00 lower at $381/00/$382.00, and palladium lost $3.00 to $147.00/$148.00.
